state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it like this: imagine you and your friend are sitting on opposite sides of a see-saw. When one side goes up, the other goes down. In the same way, alternate angles are like opposite sides of a see-saw - when one angle is big, the other is small. So, in this case, Tom is correct because alternate angles are not always equal, they just add up to 180 degrees.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get what you're saying about the see-saw and how the angles can be different. So, if angles \( p \) and \( q \) aren't always equal, does that mean they can still be different but add up to 180 degrees? I'm a bit confused about how that works with the angles in the picture. Can you explain that part again?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you and your friend are playing a game where you both have to stand on opposite sides of a line. If one person moves closer to the line, the other person has to move further away to keep the distance between you the same. In the same way, angles \( p \) and \( q \) may not always be equal, but they will always add up to 180 degrees because they are like a seesaw that balances out. So, even if they look different, they work together to make a straight line.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming alternate angles add to 180 degrees when they are actually equal only for parallel lines), fails to address the key misconception about when alternate angles are equal, provides no reasoning opportunities, and the student remains confused throughout.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (see-saw, friends standing on opposite sides of a line) to explain the abstract concept of alternate angles, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
